cards.title: Build Share of Voice, Not Rank #1
cards.summary: In answer engines the LLM summarizes many citations, so being cited most often beats being the top URL.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to optimize on a PDP, category page or landing page when you want your brand named in ChatGPT or Gemini answers for 'best X' queries.
steps: Accept the structural difference: in Google a #1 blue link 'wins' the click; in an LLM answer the model averages many citations, so the most-mentioned brand is usually named first.
Aim to appear across many citations rather than to rank one URL first.
Ethan Smith's Webflow example: they drove presence via straight SEO, YouTube videos, Reddit and blogs/affiliates — straight SEO first, YouTube second, Reddit third.
For an ecommerce store, layer the same logic: get your brand named in comparison roundups, review sites, YouTube reviews and community threads for your category, not just on your own domain.
Measure mentions across surfaces (a brand name is what gets echoed), not just clicks to your site.
caveats: Source is B2B-leaning; Webflow's specific channel ranking is one company's result, not a universal benchmark.
The named-first result is Smith's observation of behavior, not a published ranking rule.

cards.title: On-Site vs Off-Site AEO: Two Workstreams
cards.summary: Split answer-engine work into on-site pages (SEO plus long-tail product Q&A) and off-site citation groups (video, UGC, affiliates, blogs).
cards.use_when: Planning headcount or agency scope for an ecommerce brand's AEO program.
steps: On-site: do traditional SEO landing pages for high-volume keywords like 'best no-code website designer'; per Smith this free-rides into AI answers.
On-site long tail: answer highly specific product questions — use cases, features, integrations, languages, specs — because LLMs scrape detail pages and support docs.

Off-site: pursue citations in distinct groups — video (YouTube/Vimeo), UGC (Reddit, Quora), tier-1 affiliates (Dotdash Meredith titles like Good Housekeeping, Allrecipes, Investopedia), tier-2 affiliates, and blogs.
Write a separate strategy per citation group; they behave differently and need different owners.
Staffing: your SEO team handles the on-site stream; a community/generalist marketer handles video and Reddit, since most SEO people are not strong at those.

Move a help center from subdomain to subdirectory and explicitly answer obscure integration questions (e.g. 'Which meeting transcription tool integrates with Looker?') — LLMs actively scrape support docs.
caveats: Smith's claim that on-site SEO automatically produces AI visibility is an observed pattern, not a guaranteed transfer.
Subdomain-to-subdirectory moves carry their own SEO risk; validate before migrating.

cards.title: Do AEO Early Even When You Skip SEO
cards.summary: Unlike SEO, answer engines can surface a new brand within days of a citation, so early-stage and low-authority stores should prioritize AEO and skip domain-authority-dependent SEO.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend content budget for a new or low-authority ecommerce brand.
steps: Smith's standing advice for early startups: skip SEO, because you lack domain authority and it takes time to build before you can rank.
Apply the opposite logic to AEO: you can earn a citation tomorrow — a Reddit thread, a YouTube video, a blog mention — and start appearing immediately.
Recommended early-stage AEO focus: citation optimization plus long-tail questions only; skip the mid-funnel SEO work.
Cite the example: a brand-new YC company can appear in answers shortly after launch because people are talking about it.
For a new store, prioritize getting named in a handful of review threads, YouTube reviews and niche blog roundups over building a large content library.
caveats: This is Smith's strategic opinion and a change in his historical advice; it assumes you can generate genuine third-party mentions.
Spamming citations is explicitly warned against and gets detected and neutralized.

cards.title: The Long Tail Is Bigger in Chat Than in Search
cards.summary: Average chat queries run ~25 words versus ~6 for search, and include follow-ups never searched before — a large, winnable long-tail of specific product questions.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product-detail and FAQ content to write for PDPs, help centers and landing pages.
steps: Note the size difference: Smith cites roughly 25 words per query in chat versus about 6 in Google search.
Treat chat as a conversation: users ask follow-up questions, so map the whole chain of questions a buyer might ask about your product.
Include questions that have never been searched — e.g. 'which AI payment processing API integrates with X' — where competition is minimal.
For ecommerce: build PDP and help-center copy that answers the specific follow-ups around sizing, compatibility, integrations, materials, shipping, returns and use cases.
Winning this long tail is possible early for a new store because the questions are unclaimed.
The old tactic of one auto-generated page per keyword no longer works in search — but the long-tail logic has returned inside chat.
caveats: The 25-vs-6 word figures are attributed by Smith to a third party (possibly Perplexity) and are approximate.

cards.title: Improve Content With Information Gain and Typicality
cards.summary: Judge content by whether it says something nobody else said (gain) and whether it is so typical it reads as a rewrite (typicality).
cards.use_when: Editing PDP copy, buying guides or blog posts before publishing, so AI engines prefer your page over recycled competitors.
steps: Ask the two questions Smith proposes as the fix for search's rewrite-each-other problem: did you add information gain, and how typical is this page?
Information gain = something another page did not say. Add original research, tests, photography, spec comparisons or first-party data.
Typicality = how closely you mirror the existing top results. Content-scoring tools flag everything competitors already said and push you to match it — which produces the homogenized content problem.
Also demonstrate domain expertise and, where true, credentials inside the content.
Ecommerce application: instead of re-writing a competitor's buying guide, publish actual fit, durability or cost-per-use data you collected yourself.
Alignment logic: these are also what you would want ranking algorithms to reward, so writing this way serves both readers and engines.
caveats: Smith explicitly says he is not seeing Google's E-E-A-T expertise signals produce measurable effects today — treat that as an unrealized possibility, not a ranking guarantee.

cards.title: Model Collapse: Why 100% AI Content Fails
cards.summary: If AI summarizes AI-written articles, the crowd wisdom collapses and engines are eventually forced to penalize the content.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to mass-produce AI-generated product descriptions, category pages or blogs for an online store.
steps: Understand the loop: AI generates articles, other AI tools summarize them, and the underlying signal degrades because nobody added new information.
Smith's prediction: engines will eventually penalize AI content the same way they penalized scraper sites around 2007 and programmatic auto-generated landing pages after Panda.
He treats the 2007 spam-to-not-spam transition as the biggest change in his 18 years of SEO — larger than the current AEO shift.
Practical rule for a store: use AI for drafting and structure, but require a human-added information gain layer (real specs, real images, real test results).
Do not build a strategy whose durability depends on out-producing the spam filter.
Same dynamic applies inside ChatGPT: spamming the product will be detected by their search-evaluation team and neutralized.
caveats: This is a forward-looking prediction, not an observed penalty schedule; timelines are unspecified.

cards.title: Authentic Reddit Commenting for Store Visibility
cards.summary: Reddit is heavily cited by LLMs; earn it with identified, genuinely useful answers instead of fake accounts.
cards.use_when: Running community and UGC outreach to get your store named in recommendation threads that LLMs cite.
steps: Do not run the growth-hacker play of hundreds of fake accounts auto-posting and upvoting your product; Smith says it works poorly and those accounts get banned and comments deleted.
Instead: find a thread that is part of a citation you want to appear in, state who you are and where you work, and give one genuinely useful piece of information.
This is what Webflow did — a couple of employees commenting transparently.
You do not need 10,000 comments; Smith says even five good comments can be great, and it scales fine.
Reddit, Quora, Twitter and similar UGC are deliberately ranked by Google's and ChatGPT's search algorithms because the platforms want trusted user-generated content.
Ecommerce version: answer real questions in your category's subreddits about sizing, durability, or which product fits which use case.
caveats: You cannot guarantee a comment stays up — the community can remove it, so it is easy but not controllable.
Requires disclosure of affiliation; undisclosed promotion risks removal and reputational damage.

cards.title: Research the Questions Buyers Actually Ask
cards.summary: There is no search-volume truth set for chat, so derive target questions from keyword data, competitor paid search, and your own sales/support logs.
cards.use_when: Building the question list that will drive your PDP, FAQ and AEO content plan.
steps: Start with search data: take your money keywords and your competitors' — for example, look at what a rival bids on in paid search — and convert them into questions.
Paste the keyword list into ChatGPT and ask it to turn them into questions people would ask; Smith says it does a good job.
Mine internal sources for the part of the tail that never appears in search: questions asked in sales calls, customer support tickets, and on Reddit.
Assume question frequency roughly tracks keyword search volume for the overlap terms.
Accept that there is no authoritative volume data for chat questions yet — Smith expects that to change if ad products arrive.
Ecommerce application: standardize the harvested questions into an FAQ schema, PDP Q&A block and help-center articles covering the whole follow-up chain.
caveats: No volume truth set exists for chat, so you cannot weight questions by measured demand; treat it as a coverage exercise.

cards.title: Pick a Page Type That Already Gets Cited
cards.summary: Study which page formats appear in citations for your target questions and replicate that format rather than inventing one.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a category page, listicle, comparison page or tool page is the right asset to build for a target query.
steps: For each target question set, look at what is currently cited: is it a listicle, a category page, an article, or a tool page?
Choose the page type that dominates those citations and build your own version of it.
Then make it rank by answering all the follow-up and sub-topic questions in that theme — the more questions the page answers, the more likely it is to be surfaced.
If a competitor answers a sub-question and you do not, you are less likely to appear for it.

Ecommerce application: if roundups dominate for 'best X for Y', build a genuinely comparative buying guide; if category pages dominate, invest in the category template — do not default to a blog post.
Page type is decided by the citation landscape, not by what your team finds easiest to publish.
caveats: Page-type dominance is observed per query set and shifts over time; re-audit rather than locking in one template.

cards.title: Target Content Where Most Pages Deliver Nothing
cards.summary: One out of 20 landing pages drives about 85% of traffic, so concentrate budget on the few pages that can win instead of mass-producing pages.
cards.use_when: Allocating content budget across a large ecommerce catalog or content calendar.
steps: Apply Smith's analysis: roughly 1 in 20 landing pages drives about 85% of all traffic; 19 of 20 drive little to nothing.
Because most pages fail, the common tactic is spending a small amount on a large number of pages — usually via cheap non-expert rewrites of competitors' articles.
The better approach: identify the few pages that can actually win and put the full budget and best writers behind them.
Identify winners using the target-question list and the citation landscape, not gut feel.
Every dollar not spent on a doomed page is a dollar available for the top page.
Ecommerce application: audit which product or category pages drive traffic and invest in those templates and their copy first.
caveats: The 1-in-20 / 85% split is Graphite's analysis of client landing pages, not a universal law; your ratio may differ.

cards.title: Match Citation Strategy to Your Business Model
cards.summary: B2B, commerce and marketplace queries pull from different citation sources and require different measurement approaches.
cards.use_when: Choosing which review sites, publications or platforms to target for a B2B, DTC or marketplace store.
steps: Identify the citation set for your model: Smith sees TechRadar appearing heavily for B2B questions; Glamour and Cosmopolitan for commerce; Eater, Yelp and TripAdvisor for marketplaces and local.
Build your target list from the actual citations the engines return for your questions, not from generic top-domain lists.
Measurement differs: many B2B answers have nothing clickable, so last-touch referral traffic undercounts impact — you need answer tracking plus a post-conversion 'how did you hear about us' question.
Commerce does have clickable shoppable cards, so last-touch referral traffic gives a reasonable read of conversions.
For commerce cards, rich snippet schema and the number of reviews matter for appearing in the carousel.
B2B purchase cycles involve roughly dozens of touch points — nobody commits to large software from one search.
caveats: The named publications are Smith's observations of what currently appears, not fixed rules; recheck current citations.

cards.title: Set Up Answer Tracking as Share of Voice
cards.summary: Answers vary per run, per phrasing and per surface, so track distribution — how often you appear and your average rank — not a single result.
cards.use_when: Standing up measurement for AEO so you can tell whether shoppable-card, review or content changes are working.
steps: Understand the mechanics: asking the same question produces different answers each time — roughly a weighted random sample from a distribution.
Account for three variance sources: run-to-run variance, question-phrasing variance, and platform variance (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Meta).
Track share of voice: the percentage of time you appear, plus your average rank, across your tracked question set.
Ask each question multiple times and in multiple phrasings to estimate true frequency.
Tooling: answer trackers are essentially keyword trackers — many similar options exist; Smith's advice is to pick the cheapest one that meets your needs.
Prioritize surfaces by traffic rather than tracking all of them; Smith expects roughly three LLM surfaces to matter, not ten.
caveats: Recommendations to track all surfaces are impractical; Smith says you probably only need a few.
Surface popularity is unsettled — he compares it to not knowing in 1999 whether to bet only on AOL search.

cards.title: Run Controlled AEO Experiments With a Holdout
cards.summary: A before/after read is unreliable because answers drift on their own, so split your question set into test and control groups.
cards.use_when: Validating whether a Reddit campaign, YouTube review or affiliate placement actually moved your store's AI visibility.
steps: Take a large question set — Smith's example uses 200 questions — and split it into test and control.
Leave the control group completely untouched.
Intervene on the test group with one channel at a time; consider bucketing several tactics separately (Reddit comments vs. a YouTube/Vimeo video vs. a paid Forbes placement).
Allow a couple of weeks before and after the intervention to compare movement against the control group.
Only tactics where the test group rose and the control group did not are considered winners; then reproduce the study.
Reproducibility matters — Smith comes from an academic research background and warns that in SEO it is common to credit the wrong cause and then believe it forever.
Smith's framing: most best practices in SEO and AEO are unverified because people repeat claims nobody ever analyzed.
caveats: Requires enough tracked questions and time to detect a signal; small sets will be noisy.
Paid placements are controllable but expensive; Reddit is cheap but not guaranteed to stay live.

cards.title: Let AI Index You but Block Training Separately
cards.summary: Opting out of AI indexing forfeits the channel to competitors; you can refuse model training while still allowing retrieval.
cards.use_when: Making robots.txt and bot-access decisions for a store's catalog and content.
steps: Smith's position: it is not optional whether you participate — if you block indexing entirely, you simply cannot appear while competitors do.
Recognize that different bots have different purposes: training crawlers versus retrieval/index crawlers use different user agents.
Configure robots.txt so the training bot is disallowed and the index bot is allowed — Smith says this is the direct way to do it.
Alternatively use a tool or app that blocks training while permitting indexation; verify the current interface of whichever tool you choose.
Decide based on the trade-off: keeping content out of model training versus staying eligible for citation and referral traffic.
Ecommerce application: apply the same setting to catalog, help-center and buying-guide content rather than opting the whole domain out.
caveats: Bot user agents and controls change — verify current names and support before relying on a rule.
Blocking indexing forfeits visibility and is not recommended by the source as a strategy.

cards.title: AEO Traffic Converts Far Better Than Search Traffic
cards.summary: Visitors arriving from an LLM conversation have already narrowed their intent through follow-up questions, so they convert at much higher rates.
cards.use_when: Justifying investment in AI-visibility work against other acquisition channels for an ecommerce or SaaS business.
steps: Note the reported gap: Webflow saw a 6x conversion-rate difference between LLM traffic and Google search traffic.
Smith's explanation: the user has built intent through a multi-turn conversation, so they arrive pre-qualified.
Note the scale context: Webflow gets about 8% of signups from LLMs — a substantial channel, but not the largest; paid is likely still number one.
Attribution warning: users often see your brand in an answer, then open a new tab and type your brand or domain directly — your analytics will mislabel that as branded search or direct traffic.
For B2B especially, add a post-conversion 'how did you hear about us' question and use answer tracking rather than relying on referrals alone.
Still size the channel honestly: Smith says search remains larger than AEO today, even though AEO is growing.
caveats: Webflow's 6x and 8% figures are one company's results, not benchmarks you should assume.
Under-attribution is expected, so referral reports will understate the channel.

cards.title: Installation Momentum: AEO Grew Suddenly Around January
cards.summary: AEO interest stalled for months and then spiked sharply, so plan for steep, non-linear growth rather than a smooth ramp.
cards.use_when: Forecasting how fast AI-referred traffic to your store will grow when setting channel budgets.
steps: Note the pattern Smith observed: a Reforge AEO webinar a year earlier generated excitement that then died — little interest from roughly July through January.
Then activity skyrocketed in January, driven by two things: rising adoption and more clickable answers (maps, shopping carousels, clickable cards) that start appearing around that time.
Companies Graphite works with started seeing referral growth in January for the same reasons.
Smith notes this curve shape — a long flat period then a steep slope — is unusual for a new channel.
Planning implication: do not extrapolate a linear growth rate; build capability before the spike rather than after.
Practical trigger: when an engine adds new clickable formats in your category, re-check whether your products can appear in them.
caveats: Timing is Smith's observation of a specific window and will not repeat identically.
Adoption curves for AI surfaces remain uncertain.

cards.title: Tool Pricing Is Dislocated From the Work
cards.summary: Smith calls out AI-visibility tooling as unusually expensive for tasks that are essentially commodity keyword tracking.
cards.use_when: Evaluating what to pay for AEO tracking or content tooling for your store.
steps: Apply the sanity test Smith uses: imagine being charged $50,000 for keyword tracking — you would call it absurd because you could write it yourself.
The same commodity work is being sold at high prices in the AEO category because the mechanics feel mysterious and the growth curve looks steep.
Before signing, identify what the tool actually does and whether it is a renamed version of a known commodity task.
Default to the cheapest tool that meets your needs — there is no premium tier of ranking; you either appear or you do not.
Spend the saved budget on the citation work that actually moves visibility: content, video, affiliate placements and community participation.
Verify current pricing and capabilities directly, since the category is changing quickly.
caveats: This is Smith's market opinion; some tools may carry genuine costs (API calls at scale) that justify higher prices.

cards.title: Google Search Is Not Dying — Reject the Cycle of Panic
cards.summary: New channels add on top of search rather than taking Google's share, so do not reallocate your whole budget on the strength of news headlines.
cards.use_when: Responding to internal pressure to defund organic or search spend because 'AI killed Google.'
steps: Recognize the recurring pattern Smith describes: every couple of years articles claim Google search is dying because of a new thing — previously TikTok search, before that Instagram, Facebook and YouTube.
The pattern is not that these channels are fake; people do search and discover on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram — but those channels add on top rather than subtract from Google.
Smith's framing: Google's slice of the pie stays the same, while the pie gets bigger.
Evidence he cites: Google's VP of search said publisher traffic from Google is not down and is up slightly.
For an ecommerce brand: keep the search channel funded, and add AEO as an additional channel rather than a replacement.
Treat claims that AI has destroyed search traffic as something to verify in your own analytics before acting.
caveats: Smith is an SEO-business owner and argues from within that industry; verify the traffic claims against your own data.

cards.title: LLM Mechanics: RAG vs. Model Training
cards.summary: Most controllable AEO work happens in the retrieval layer (search plus summarization), not in model weights.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest effort when trying to influence what an AI assistant says about your products.
steps: Understand the two layers: the core model, trained on large web corpora, performs next-word prediction (e.g. the capital of California).
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) performs a live search and then summarizes the results — this is the layer that produces citations.
Almost everything actionable in AEO lives in RAG; influencing the core model is extremely hard and may take a year or more to show.
Importantly, Smith expects a model will probably not name your product if it never appeared in any retrieved results — so RAG presence is the foundation.
Practical implication for a store: prioritize being present in the retrievable set (review sites, comparisons, video, communities, your own indexed pages) over trying to influence training data.
Skip the obscure tactic of mass-producing pages that assert a brand is best for a keyword; Smith says few would want to spend time on it.
caveats: RAG-versus-training behavior is Smith's working model of these systems and may not describe every product's architecture.
